summary: A memo by John McCarthy on how documents with arbitrary characters could be stored, shown, edited and printed on any equipment. It reviews where things stood: 96-character ASCII, many sites on 64-character sets, and Stanford's larger character set. It then proposes how to move toward a larger shared set, with special reference to the ARPANET.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 373 proposes a way to identify characters that different computers could display or print. Registries would give characters and character sets shared descriptions, while each device would convert them into its own form.

questions: how to share character designs across networks
what problem did arbitrary character sets address
how would the character registry work
subtitle: A proposal for sharing expanded character sets across systems

tldr.problem: Computers and devices used different character sets, making it hard to exchange documents containing characters not available everywhere.
tldr.mechanism: John McCarthy proposes registries for individual characters and character sets, plus mappings from those descriptions to local device formats.
tldr.outcome: The memo argues for registering character designs first and leaving typography questions for later discussion.

today: RFC 373 is a proposal for character and character-set registries. It presents an approach for discussion and does not describe an adopted registry.

sections.title: Different Machines, Different Character Sets
sections.content:
John McCarthy describes systems that support different character sets. The memo notes that some installations used 64-character sets, while others used 96-character ASCII; Stanford's AI Laboratory had a 114-character set that included ASCII. The goal is to exchange documents with arbitrary characters across devices.

McCarthy argues against first trying to agree on one expanded fixed character set, because equipment might not adopt it.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers could not show all the characters used by others. The memo proposes a way to refer to characters without requiring every device to use the same local codes.

sections.title: Registries for Characters and Sets
sections.content:
The proposal creates a registry in which each character has a unique number, an ASCII name and a design shown on a 50-by-50 dot matrix. A separate registry would describe character sets by mapping their bit sequences to registered character numbers.

A document would identify the character code it uses. It could also include a table of mappings or use an escape character to refer to a character by its registry number.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared registry would give each character a number, name and dot design. A character-set table would explain how a local code refers to those registered characters.

sections.title: Adapting Characters to Devices
sections.content:
Printers and displays render characters in different ways, so the proposal leaves device-specific conversion to the programs that support each device. These programs could use hand-built mappings, convert from registered character designs, or combine both methods.

The memo also discusses the extra difficulty of displays that share character memory and says typography, such as different fonts, should be left for later.
sections.plainLanguage: Each printer or display would need a way to turn shared character descriptions into shapes it can show. The proposal sets typography aside as a separate problem.
